Series::frexp¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

std::pair<Series, Series> Series::frexp() const

What It Does¶

Splits each element x into a normalized fraction and a power-of-two exponent:

x == mantissa * 2^exponent,   with 0.5 <= |mantissa| < 1   (both 0 when x == 0)

This is the elementwise form of C’s frexp. It is the exact inverse of ldexp(): mantissa.ldexp(exponent) reconstructs x bit for bit. Use it to inspect or rescale the binary magnitude of a series without touching its significant digits — for example to bring a batch of values into a common exponent before summing, or to implement a stable log or a custom float format.

The return is a std::pair<Series, Series> — a fixed arity of two, so a pair rather than a single value:

  • .first is the mantissa, same shape and floating dtype as the input (Float32 -> Float32, Float64 -> Float64)

  • .second is the exponent, same shape, dtype int32

Structured bindings work: auto [m, e] = x.frexp();.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

std::pair<Series, Series> {mantissa, exponent}. The mantissa keeps the input’s floating dtype; the exponent is int32.

Raises if the input is not a floating-point series.

Gradient¶

The mantissa is differentiable within each interval where the exponent remains constant:

d mantissa / d x = 2^(-exponent)

The integer exponent is non-differentiable. At a boundary where the selected exponent changes, the reported sensitivity is the derivative of the local mantissa branch rather than a derivative through the discontinuous exponent.

Examples¶

Example 1. The fraction is always in [0.5, 1) in magnitude; the exponent carries the binary scale.

auto [mantissa, exponent] =
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 6.0, 0.75, 0.0, -8.0}).frexp();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, mantissa) << '\n';
pluss::series::print(std::cout, exponent);

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5000, 0.7500, 0.7500, 0.0000, -0.5000]
Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=int32, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 3, 0, 0, 4]

1 = 0.5 * 2^1, 6 = 0.75 * 2^3, 0.75 = 0.75 * 2^0, 0 maps to (0, 0), and -8 = -0.5 * 2^4.

Example 2. frexp() and ldexp() are inverses.

auto [m, e] = pluss::make_series({3.0, 100.0, 0.1}).frexp();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, m.ldexp(e));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3.0000, 100.0000, 0.1000]

Example 3. Reverse through the mantissa uses the exponent selected for each element.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 6.0, 0.75, -8.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
auto [m, e] = x.frexp();
m.sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5000, 0.1250, 1.0000, 0.0625]

Those values are 2^-1, 2^-3, 2^0, and 2^-4. The sign of the input does not change the local scale factor.

Example 4. A non-floating input raises.

try {
  auto [m, e] = pluss::make_series({1, 2, 3}).frexp();
  pluss::series::print(std::cout, m);
} catch (const std::exception& err) {
  std::string msg = err.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

frexp: floating-point input required

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The exponent is int32, not int64.

  • frexp(0) is (0, 0); the mantissa is not forced onto [0.5, 1) for a zero input.

  • Integer and boolean series raise frexp: floating-point input required; convert with to() first.

  • Only the mantissa carries sensitivity; the integer exponent does not.

  • The mantissa sign matches the input sign (frexp(-8) = (-0.5, 4)), so |mantissa| is what lies in [0.5, 1).

Summary¶

frexp() decomposes x into mantissa * 2^exponent:

  • returns std::pair<Series, Series> = {mantissa (float), exponent (int32)}

  • |mantissa| in [0.5, 1); (0, 0) for a zero input

  • the exact inverse of ldexp()

  • floating-point input only; mantissa differentiable within each exponent band

See Also¶

  • Series::ldexp: the inverse — mantissa * 2^exponent.

  • Series::log2: the continuous analogue of the exponent.

  • Series::sort: another method returning a std::pair<Series, Series>.
